1:
The instrument is a sword, not a knife. Ellicott would render it take thee a sharp sword and use it as a barber's razor, noting that the same word recurs in the next verse translated both ways; a weapon is picked up for its symbolism and put to a barber's work. Clarke reaches the same result from the period's toolkit, where edge-tools were few and the sword served as knife and razor by turns. Gill allows it the general sense of anything that cuts asunder.

Ellicott adds the detail that gives the act its edge. Shaving was a common sign of mourning, but the nearer allusion is the older prophet's picture of judgment as a shaving with a hired razor; and Ezekiel was a priest, forbidden by the law to shave head or beard. A priest shorn with a sword announced a desolation of the first order. Henry gathers the other associations: the ignominy put on humiliated envoys, the head shaved in mourning, the end of the Nazarite's vow, the city no longer holy. Wesley compresses all three into mourning, reproach and deformity.

Henry makes the man himself the sign, reading his willingness as evidence that he did not want the day he foretold. The hair carries the argument. A capital that had been the head degenerated into hair, which grown thick is a burden its owner wishes rid of, and the sentence echoes the complaint about easing oneself of adversaries. Not the superfluous growth only but all of it goes, marking a full end; hair that would not be kept trim by the warnings of prophets comes off altogether. Those will be ruined, Henry concludes, that will not be reformed.

The balances are not decoration. Henry takes them for a justice that weighs men and actions without error and apportions different penalties to different offenders. Clarke says the same in a line; Ellicott insists the weighing proves the certainty of what is coming rather than making the scene vivid. Calvin wants the equity: a true balance, so that no portion outweighs another. He also presses what hair represents: a multitude past counting, which was the city's boast, its numbers breeding the confidence that destroyed it; and since not a hair is left, not a man escapes.

The three portions are decoded much alike. Clarke sets out the allegory in order: the prophet the nation, his hair the people, the razor the invader, the division the kinds of punishment. Burning within the city means those consumed by famine and plague; the portion struck about the walls, those killed in sorties and in the storming; the scattered portion, the deported, the sword drawn after because exile would not end the danger. Henry adds that the burning of the city might itself count as a third of the ruin, and that the sword found the defenders when the besiegers were fiercest. Ellicott thinks the burning was described rather than performed, and notes plain prediction beginning to mix with symbol, the drawn sword lifted from the law's curses.

The handful bound in the skirts matters most. Gill identifies them with the vinedressers left behind by the captain of the guard and those who came back from Egypt. Ellicott traces their fate to the disorders that followed, from which a fire spread through the whole house, ending in a land emptied of its people; he marks this as the point where symbol gives way to the parallelisms of Hebrew verse. Calvin sees the covenant at stake: a seed had to be kept or the nation would have gone the way of Sodom, and the survivors are tucked into a garment's fold to show it. But some of that handful burn, which tells him how desperate the impiety was, and warns the escaped against supposing their troubles over. Wesley names the causes of that second fire: their own quarrels and conspiracies.
5:
Naming the sign is ordinary scriptural usage, Henry says: the thing signified lends its name to the sign, as at the supper. The shaved head stands for a city stripped of ornament, emptied and left bare, and a priest's head best fits a holy city. Gill lets the identification cover both signs, the drawing on the tile and the shorn head, and calls the place chief not merely of its own country. Keil and Delitzsch head these verses as the divine word explaining the symbols by giving the cause, with the execution beginning further on.

Being set among the nations is read first as honour. Henry denies it was a remote corner, describes cultivated neighbours famous for learning, then presses two senses: the city was raised above them as a hill above hills, watched by all around in goodwill or malice, and set like a candle on a stand to carry light outward, so that observers might judge the people wise from their laws. Had the reputation held, the blessing would have spread; failing that, the design waited for the day when the word went out into all nations, after which the city itself was levelled.

Ellicott turns the position into a map and an argument. Egypt lay south, the Hittites and later the Syrians and Assyrians north, Philistines and Phoenicians along the coast, the caravan traders east; even trade with India had been opened. A people so placed could have shown the world a nation prosperous under one God and become the missionary of that faith, while deserts, sea and mountains fenced them enough to grow undisturbed. Once the bond of unity weakened, the same position made them prey — subject to petty tribes in the era of the judges, later a ball kicked between two empires, taxed as friends or wasted as enemies. Responsibility, he concludes, is proportioned to privilege.

Calvin insists the praise is not praise. God recites his benefits to reprove, since the greater the gifts the baser the ingratitude, and contempt of them is sacrilege; the city stands on a platform so that its dignity shows from every side, and that visibility completes its disgrace. He refuses the reading that makes the phrase a claim about the earth's exact centre, calling the fancy puerile, and takes the sense to be the most celebrated part of the world, the sea near, Egypt neighbouring, Babylon north. The demonstrative is emphatic: the city is the most beautiful part of a theatre, drawing every eye. Clarke entertains the geographical claim, allows it roughly defensible, then observes that the true land centre of a hemisphere falls on the capital of his own empire.

The charge itself turns on a verb. Gill reports that the word may mean rebelled against or transgressed rather than changed, though the older Jewish authorities keep changed; Ellicott prefers wickedly resisted, the sense most modern expositors adopt, and reads the closing pronoun of the Israelites, not the heathen. Calvin agrees that reject is the commoner force, and adds that a fault with some pretext of virtue might be extenuated while gross impiety against known commandments cannot.

Whether they were worse than the heathen divides the tile sharply. Clarke says plainly that they were: idolatrous as the neighbours were, they kept more morality than the Jews had, and men who fall from a height become more abominable in proportion to it, which he calls the common case of backsliders. Ellicott denies the comparison as stated, holding the Israelites were in fact far better than the surrounding heathen and the sentence relative to the light given; he compares the towns the Lord upbraided, which nobody supposes matched Sodom. Calvin lands between them, making the aggravation lie in knowledge — a yoke shaken off knowingly, no excuse left once instruction has come from the divine mouth, and blessings appointed for salvation turned to destruction.
7:
The verb behind multiplied is disputed. Ellicott would render it raged, the sense it carries in the psalm about the nations and the one the lexicons give, so that the charge is self-will and opposition rather than numbers. Calvin canvasses three readings. One joins the clause into a single thought, that prosperity made them wanton as an overfed horse turns restive, and cites the song of Moses about a well-fed Israel kicking; Calvin rejects it as forced. Another derives the word from a root meaning to be agitated, giving a people tumultuous beyond all nations and drawn on unbridled; that he calls far-fetched. He settles for the plain sense of increase. Wesley takes the increase to be in idols and superstitions rather than in people.

The following clause about the judgments of the nations is genuinely ambiguous, and Ellicott sets out both readings. It may mean that Israel failed to keep even the natural laws the heathen observed, which would make them worse in actual conduct than their neighbours; or that Israel failed to keep revealed laws as faithfully as the heathen kept what nature and tradition taught them. He prefers the second, on the ground that behaving exactly as the heathen behaved would already be a far deeper unfaithfulness in a people given more. Wesley takes the first without hesitation: exceeding them in superstition and idolatry, falling short of them in the moral virtues. Gill simply notes that the sins having been set out, the sentence now follows.

The doubled pronoun draws comment. Gill hears the omnipotent king declaring himself an adversary, and asks what is more terrible than to have the mighty God against you. Calvin agrees the repetition is emphatic, meant to put fear into the hearers, and then twice refuses the older interpretation. It does not mean that angels and human agents are excluded because the destruction is to be direct, for the Assyrians and Chaldeans were plainly used as scourges; nor does the phrase about executing judgments assert that the punishment will be measured and not too rigid. To execute judgment, Calvin says, means simply to exercise jurisdiction.

Ellicott ties the publicity of the sentence back to the position of the city. A people set conspicuously among the nations, whose unfaithfulness every neighbour had watched, must have its punishment seen by the same audience; the visibility that was privilege becomes the condition of the judgment.

What remains is the claim that nothing like it had been done before or would be again. Gill lists what it therefore outdoes: the flood, the fire on Sodom, the plagues in Egypt, the expulsion of the Canaanites. Wesley finds the difference in duration, since water and fire both kill quickly and this would not. Clarke reads it as a comparison of catastrophes and names two, the sack under Nebuchadnezzar and the far worse one under Titus, calling them unparalleled in human history. Ellicott rejects that whole approach: the comparison is not between one judgment on this people and another, nor need the later destruction be in view at all, but between God's dealings with them and with everyone else, so that the whole long series of judgments comes into view together. Calvin explains why the ordinary measure had to be exceeded — common punishments are despised — and refuses to read the horror that follows as metaphor merely because interpreters could find no record of it, appealing to the historian's account of mothers who ate their own children.
10:
Parents eating children is treated as fact, not figure. Gill traces the threat to the law and the fulfilment to three sieges, the last reported by the historian of the Roman war, and reasons that though the recorded cases are of mothers, fathers must have shared: if the tenderer parent could do it, the other surely did. Clarke concedes that history does not state it so precisely but refuses to doubt it given the extremities, and points to the lament about women boiling their own children. Calvin works from the same passage, noting that it singles out women not merely as mothers but as the more humane by nature, so that their doing it is the final portent.

The scattering is meant to leave nothing. Calvin observes that a surviving name or body of the people would have been ground for hope, and that is what is refused. Clarke reads it as deportation among all nations, and Wesley finds it verified twice, in those carried off after the besiegers withdrew and in the last company that fled into Egypt.

An oath follows, which Gill notes is the form that makes revocation impossible, and a reason Wesley reduces to two words: the temple, and the idols in it. Calvin agrees: corrupted religion and a violated sanctuary are why the vengeance is pressed so hard. Ellicott insists on the symmetry of the clauses — nothing is inflicted that was not called down — and corrects the verb that follows. Diminish is inadequate and its pronoun has nothing behind it; the verb means to withdraw, reflexively or with the eye of the next clause as object, and either way what is withdrawn is presence and compassion.

Then the figure is resolved into plain speech. Gill matches the burning third to those consumed by plague and hunger, Clarke refers back to his own key. Calvin points out what the resolution omits: the fourth portion, hidden in the fold of the garment, is not mentioned again, though it was not spoken in vain, God varying his manner by his own right while figure and application still agree.

The clause about being comforted divides them sharpest. Ellicott notes the word can mean either to feel compassion, and so relent, or to console oneself by vengeance, and judges the second intended: honour wounded by a chosen people's sins and mocked among the heathen is vindicated publicly. Calvin reports interpreters who took the verse for a promise of pardon and rejects them, since what follows will not bear it. Wesley agrees in a phrase: comfort in executing vengeance, zeal for the divine glory. Gill hears completion, a threat long deferred with only drops falling before, now poured out to the last; Clarke adds that the displeasure is not transient but settled.

The closing catalogue is read for its images. Calvin prefers the sense of drought in the word for waste, and thinks the disgrace attested not by rumour only but by every traveller; the pair of nouns for reproach and taunt implies slaughter, since scorn needs a ground. Wesley turns the taunt into a proverb and the ruin into a lesson. Gill offers three ways to take the arrows of famine — hunger shot from the divine quiver, the causes that bring it, or the wasting it produces — while Clarke recalls that the ancients drew famine and plague as poisoned shafts. Calvin makes the archer deliberate rather than ornamental, chosen to pierce minds like stone; the arrows are deadly because a man may survive an ordinary wound and not these. On the beasts Gill and Clarke part: Gill insists on literal lions and wolves threatened in the law, Clarke that wild animals multiply where a country is emptied, adding that the invader, often likened to a lion, may be meant. Wesley looks past the nearer ruin to a final one.
